--- ## 1. Understand the experiment Think of a student solving a math problem on paper. In 03, we supplied a worked solution and taught the student to predict its words. Here, the student writes its **own** solution. After each partial answer, the teacher tells us how likely each possible next token should be. A token is a small piece of text, sometimes a whole word and sometimes only part of one. The teacher is **frozen**, so its weights never change. Only the small student learns. The teacher's probabilities are guidance about text, not a guarantee that the arithmetic is correct. A teacher can still prefer a wrong continuation. | Starting point | Additional practice | Purpose | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Starting SFT** | None | Measure the checkpoint we already have | | **Continued SFT** | 1,024 new reference solutions | Check what more ordinary supervised practice achieves | | **On-policy KD** | The same 1,024 questions, student-written responses, teacher distributions | Test learning on prefixes the student actually visits | The full training recipe starts both arms from **identical checkpoint bytes**, uses the same question order, and makes 128 optimizer updates with eight examples per update. The next EOS comparison stops each fresh KD pilot after at most 32 updates. Their token counts, compute cost, and learning signals differ. This comparison measures the two methods together with their different learning signals and token budgets. Isolating the sampling policy would require another arm. ![Three arms from the same checkpoint](assets/04_on_policy_distillation/controlled_comparison.png) ### How this relates to the paper We implement the fully on-policy case of [GKD, Section 3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2306.13649v3#S3.SS1): sample from the current student, hold those token IDs fixed, and match the teacher's next-token distributions on those prefixes. We use **forward KL** and teacher temperature `0.1`, following its arithmetic experiment choices. Our Qwen models, reference-solution warm start, prompt, data budget, and training scale are different. This is an educational adaptation, not the paper's reported benchmark experiment. **On-policy** describes where responses come from, not the direction of KL. 01 used reverse KL to inspect mechanics. 04 uses forward KL for this experiment. Teacher-generated answers are used only to measure teacher validation performance. Training targets come from teacher distributions on student-written prefixes. This experiment uses full student fine-tuning with no answer filtering.

### 1.1 What the first run taught us

The original shared plain-text prompt produced a misleading learning signal.
Detailed logs contain 52 updates. Every response from updates 24 through 52 hit
the 256-token cap, with examples that repeat words or restart the question.
Reference-token validation loss increased even while fixed-prefix KL decreased.

A user-run A100 probe scored the **same early response** under two teacher contexts.
At its final position, combined stopping probability changed from about
$3.93\times10^{-8}$ with the raw prompt to **0.530** with non-thinking chat
formatting. At target temperature 0.1, chat stopping mass was approximately **0.777**.
The observed student EOS itself stayed unlikely. The teacher preferred its own
`im_end` token. Both token IDs are valid stopping events for our student.

This single probe supports a teacher-context explanation. It does not establish
that a corrected training run will improve accuracy. The example response was
itself arithmetically wrong, illustrating why stopping and correctness need
separate measurements.

![Observed failure and teacher stopping probe](assets/04_on_policy_distillation/observed_failure.png)

*Measured evidence from the interrupted experiment and one response-boundary probe.
The dashed response-length ceiling is the configured generation budget.*

The [archived evidence](assets/04_on_policy_distillation/recorded_failure/manifest.json)
and [investigation](assets/04_on_policy_distillation/INVESTIGATION.md) preserve
this failure. Later console output reaches update 61, while complete downloaded
trajectories and history cover only updates 1 through 52.

### The follow-up Amarel pilot

With non-thinking teacher context, the teacher reached **52/64 strict validation
matches**, compared with **32/64** for the starting student and **40/64** for the
completed continued-SFT control. Alignment checks passed. During distillation,
responses became longer and more repetitive. The guard paused at update 22,
when **24 of the latest 32 responses** reached the 256-token cap. SLURM then ended
the allocation during follow-up validation. Reference loss had risen from 0.667
to 0.819 at update 16 while fixed-prefix KL fell.

The next hypothesis concerns how the loss interprets ending tokens. The student
learned `endoftext`, while earlier teacher probes preferred `im_end`. Both end
this single-turn response, but raw-token KL still compares their probabilities
separately. The next controlled comparison changes only that interpretation.
Its results will test how much ending-token disagreement contributes to the failure.
[Recorded Amarel evidence](assets/04_on_policy_distillation/recorded_amarel_pilot/README.md)

### 3.1 What exactly receives a loss?

`input_ids` contains prompt tokens followed by response tokens. For SFT, the
response comes from the reference solution. For on-policy KD, it comes from the
student. Prompt positions provide context but have no direct training loss. Processing
that context still affects how the student predicts its response.

We process one unpadded response at a time during distillation. This removes the
need to guess which repeated end-token IDs are padding. SFT still uses explicit
`-100` labels to ignore prompt/padding positions. A real end token remains a target.

![The one-token prediction relationship](assets/04_on_policy_distillation/token_alignment.png)

If the prompt has `P` tokens, the first response token is at complete-sequence
index `P`, but its prediction is at logits index `P - 1`. The last prompt token's
logits predict what comes next. We therefore keep `logits[:, P - 1:-1, :]`.
The final logits position predicts an unobserved token and is excluded.

--- ## 7. Qualify the teacher and prove response alignment The teacher receives its non-thinking chat question context, followed by the **exact response IDs the student generated**. Its prefix length is $P_T$, while the student's is $P_S$. Their first-response predictions occur at $P_T-1$ and $P_S-1$, respectively. The aligned response-logit tensors both have shape $[1,R,V]$ even when their complete-sequence lengths differ. For example, the same response IDs for `3 + 2 = 5` follow a plain `Answer:` prefix for the student and an assistant-turn prefix for the teacher. We append those IDs directly, avoiding changed token boundaries from decoding and retokenizing them. We also generate teacher answers on the **64 validation questions** to measure its format, numeric matching, and stopping behavior under this context. These answers are never substituted into distillation training. Greater model size and higher stopping probability alone do not prove useful arithmetic supervision. `eval()` selects inference behavior. `requires_grad_(False)` freezes parameters, and `torch.no_grad()` prevents a teacher gradient graph. Each checkpoint receives the same questions, prompt, greedy decoding, end-token rules, token budget, and frozen answer checkers. References are used **after generation** to score the final number. - **Strict match** counts a correct numeric answer on the required `#### ` final line. - **Format compliance** counts a parseable final line, whether its number is right or wrong. - **Exploratory prose match** uses the unchanged broader extractor to find a matching final number. - **Token-limit stops** count responses that exhausted the budget without a recognized end token. We keep every question in the denominator. A higher format score alone is not better arithmetic. Numeric agreement also does not establish valid reasoning. Paired bootstrap intervals summarize uncertainty across these questions, conditional on one training seed. They do not measure run-to-run training variability. ### What we achieved, in the simplest terms

**01** followed one student answer through scoring, KL, gradients, and one update.
The saved update increased KL. It demonstrated mechanics and exposed limitations.

**02** measured the original student and separated format compliance from numeric
agreement. The checkers and original responses remain inspectable.

**03** taught the student from 256 worked examples and saved a verified checkpoint.
It learned the answer format strongly. Reasoning results remained mixed.

**04** exposed a real failure in teacher feedback. The student increasingly kept
writing even as its KL fell. A frozen-teacher probe showed that chat formatting
changed stopping probabilities on one saved prefix. The corrected-context Amarel
pilot passed alignment checks and performed 22 updates, then reached the stopping
health guard. The continued-SFT control completed 128 updates and scored 40/64
strict validation matches. The new experiment compares two interpretations of EOS
tokens, with separate student policies and recoverable progress.

**Current evidence boundary** · The recorded failures, teacher probes, and completed
SFT control are user-run GPU evidence. Local CPU checks test the new grouped loss,
gradients, and recovery behavior using small random models. The new 32-update EOS
comparison and fixed full-run test remain pending on Amarel. Whether this change
stabilizes stopping or improves answers remains an experimental question.

After a successful full run, inspect strict matches, format compliance, prose
matches, capped responses, paired uncertainty, and changed answers together.
Neither teacher confidence nor a lower KL alone proves better reasoning.

KD arm using the same divergence would help isolate the effect of student-generated
prefixes. The reported bootstrap interval covers question-sampling uncertainty
